topics.name: Main sequence
topics.kicker: Hydrogen-fusing band on the H–R diagram · Where stars spend most of their lives
topics.dates: Found on the first H–R diagrams, 1911–1913
topics.briefing: Plot stars by brightness and temperature, and most of them fall along one diagonal stripe: the main sequence. A star joins it when it starts fusing hydrogen into helium in its core and stays there for about 90 percent of its life; heavier stars sit higher on the stripe and burn out faster. The Sun has been on the main sequence for about 4.6 billion years and has roughly 5 billion to go.
topics.answerHtml: main sequence (accept main-sequence stars; prompt on dwarf stars or luminosity class V; do not accept “Hertzsprung–Russell diagram,” “red giants,” or “white dwarfs”)

tossups.p: Stars on this band stay stable because the outward push of their hot gas balances the inward pull of gravity, a state called hydrostatic equilibrium. Annie Jump Cannon’s spectral classes O, B, A, F, G, K, and M run along this band, from its hottest stars to its coolest.
tossups.r: The Sun lies on this band. For 10 points, name this diagonal band on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, where stars fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores.

tossups.p: The lower end of this band lies at about 8 percent of the Sun’s mass, because smaller objects called brown dwarfs never get hot enough inside to keep fusing ordinary hydrogen. The coolest, dimmest stars on this band are red dwarfs, such as Proxima Centauri.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this band on the H–R diagram that holds the Sun and most other stars.

tossups.p: The smallest stars on this band, red dwarfs with less than about a third of the Sun’s mass, are stirred by convection all the way through, so they can use up most of their hydrogen. Such stars may stay on this band for trillions of years, far longer than the universe has existed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this longest stage of a star’s life, when it fuses hydrogen into helium in its core.

tossups.p: Stars on the upper part of this band, with more than about 1.3 times the Sun’s mass, get most of their energy from the CNO cycle, in which carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen nuclei act as catalysts. Stars on its lower part, including the Sun, mostly use the proton-proton chain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this band on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, where stars spend most of their lives fusing hydrogen.

tossups.p: Blue stragglers are odd stars in star clusters that still sit on this band, even though they lie above the cluster’s turnoff point, where heavier stars have already peeled away. Astronomers find a cluster’s age from that turnoff, because heavier stars leave this band first.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this diagonal band of hydrogen-fusing stars on the H–R diagram, which includes the Sun.

tossups.p: By sliding a star cluster’s diagram up or down until its version of this band lines up with a standard one, astronomers can work out how far away the cluster is. Newborn stars land on the “zero-age” edge of this band when hydrogen fusion first switches on in their cores.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this band on the H–R diagram, where stars spend about 90 percent of their lives.

tossups.p: In the Morgan–Keenan system, stars on this band get the Roman numeral V and are called dwarfs, even though the hottest of them are several times wider than the Sun. The Sun’s full label, G2 V, places it near the middle of this band.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this band on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, where stars fuse hydrogen in their cores.

tossups.p: For stars on this band, luminosity rises roughly as mass to the 3.5 power, so a star ten times as massive as the Sun shines thousands of times brighter and uses up its core hydrogen in only tens of millions of years. The hottest, bluest stars on this band sit at its upper left.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this band on the H–R diagram that runs from the upper left to the lower right.

tossups.p: Stars that have just left this band drift to the right across the H–R diagram as subgiants. In about five billion years, the Sun will use up the hydrogen in its core, leave this band, and swell into a red giant.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this stage of a star’s life, when it steadily fuses hydrogen into helium in its core.

tossups.p: Stars slowly brighten while they are on this band, because helium builds up in their cores. Early in its time on this band, the Sun gave off only about 70 percent as much energy as it does in modern times, which leads to a puzzle called the faint young Sun paradox.
tossups.r: Most stars, including the Sun, lie on it. For 10 points, name this diagonal band on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram.

tossups.p: Vega, the brightest star in Lyra, and Sirius A, the brightest star in the night sky, are both hot, white stars on this band. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, is a dim red dwarf near this band’s lower right end.
tossups.r: Red supergiants like Betelgeuse have already left it. For 10 points, name this band on the H–R diagram, where stars fuse hydrogen in their cores.

tossups.p: All stars on this band are sometimes called dwarf stars, a name that covers yellow stars like the Sun and red dwarfs but not white dwarfs or brown dwarfs. Roughly 90 percent of all stars belong to this band.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this band on the H–R diagram, where stars fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores.

tossups.p: Newborn stars creep toward this band along Hayashi tracks, which run almost straight down the H–R diagram, and the heavier ones finish the trip along Henyey tracks, which run to the left. The Sun has been on this band for about 4.6 billion years.
tossups.r: A star joins it once hydrogen fusion begins in its core. For 10 points, name this band on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram.

tossups.p: When Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell separately plotted stars’ brightness against their colors or spectral types in the early 1910s, most stars fell along this narrow band. The most massive stars on this band leave it after only a few million years, while the Sun will spend about 10 billion years on it in all.
tossups.r: It runs from hot, blue stars at the upper left to cool, red stars at the lower right. For 10 points, name this band.

tossups.p: By timing the orbits of binary stars, astronomers weighed stars on this band and found that their masses rise steadily toward its upper left, from less than a tenth of the Sun’s mass to more than fifty times. Massive stars on this band have churning, convective cores.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this band on the H–R diagram where stars, including the Sun, fuse hydrogen into helium.

clues.t: Stars on it fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores
A diagonal band across the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, from hot, bright, blue stars at the upper left to cool, dim, red stars at the lower right
The Sun is on it, about halfway through its stay of roughly 10 billion years
Roughly 90 percent of stars belong to it, and stars spend about 90 percent of their lives on it
A star’s place on it depends mostly on its mass: the heaviest, hottest stars sit at the upper left
Luminosity rises roughly as mass to the 3.5 power, so a star ten times the Sun’s mass shines thousands of times brighter
Heavier stars leave it sooner: the most massive last only a few million years, while red dwarfs may last trillions of years
When its core hydrogen runs out, a star leaves it and swells into a red giant; the Sun will do so in about five billion years
Its stars stay stable because outward gas pressure balances gravity, a state called hydrostatic equilibrium
Its stars are called dwarfs, class V in the Morgan–Keenan system, so the Sun’s full label is G2 V
Red dwarfs such as Proxima Centauri sit at its lower right; hot O and B stars sit at its upper left
A star cluster’s age comes from its turnoff point, where its stars are peeling away from this band
Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell found most stars on this band when they plotted brightness against color in the early 1910s
Annie Jump Cannon’s spectral classes O, B, A, F, G, K, M run along it, from the hottest stars at the upper left to the coolest at the lower right
Its lower end is about 8 percent of the Sun’s mass (roughly 80 times Jupiter’s); smaller brown dwarfs can’t keep fusing ordinary hydrogen
Stars above about 1.3 Suns mostly use the CNO cycle; the Sun and smaller stars mostly use the proton-proton chain
Red dwarfs below about a third of the Sun’s mass are fully convective, stirring their hydrogen through their whole interior
Massive stars on it have convective cores; in Sun-like stars, energy leaves the core mainly as radiation
Stars first land on its “zero-age” edge when hydrogen fusion switches on in their cores
Newborn stars reach it along Hayashi tracks (almost straight down) and, for heavier ones, Henyey tracks (to the left)
Sliding a cluster’s version of this band up or down to match a standard one gives the cluster’s distance, a method called “fitting”
Blue stragglers sit on it above a cluster’s turnoff, even though stars that heavy should already have left
Stars slowly brighten on it as helium builds up; the early Sun gave off only about 70 percent of its modern energy (the faint young Sun paradox)
Vega and Sirius A are hot, white stars on it; red supergiants like Betelgeuse have already left it
Orbits of binary stars show that its stars range from under a tenth of the Sun’s mass to more than fifty times
Stars that have just left it drift to the right across the H–R diagram as subgiants

trap.title: Band, diagram, or dwarf?
trap.body: Tossups on this band are full of H–R diagram clues, so players buzz with “Hertzsprung–Russell diagram,” which is the whole graph, not the band of stars on it. Others answer “red giants,” the stage that comes after it. The word “dwarf” causes more trouble: the Sun (a yellow dwarf) and red dwarfs are on this band, but white dwarfs and brown dwarfs are not.
trap.fix: “This band,” “this stage,” hydrogen fusing into helium in the core, the turnoff, or the zero-age line means main sequence. “This diagram” or “this graph” means the H–R diagram. Saying only “dwarf stars” earns a prompt, so give the full name.
trap.line: Real answer line: main sequence (accept main-sequence stars; do not accept “Hertzsprung–Russell diagram” or “red giants”)

topics.name: White dwarfs
topics.kicker: Earth-sized leftover cores of Sun-like stars · Held up by electron pressure
topics.dates: Sirius B first seen 1862; name coined 1922
topics.briefing: When a star like the Sun runs out of fuel, it puffs its outer layers into space and leaves behind its hot, glowing core: a white dwarf. A typical white dwarf squeezes more than half the Sun’s mass into a ball about the size of Earth, so a piece the size of a sugar cube would weigh about a ton. With no fuel left to burn, it slowly cools and fades over billions of years.
topics.answerHtml: white dwarfs (accept degenerate dwarfs; prompt on dwarfs or stellar remnants; do not accept “red dwarfs,” “brown dwarfs,” “black dwarfs,” or “neutron stars”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: While sailing from India to England in 1930, a 19-year-old student realized that these objects have a maximum possible mass, which modern calculations put at about 1.4 times the Sun’s. Arthur Eddington publicly rejected that idea, but its discoverer later shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.
tossups.r: That limit is named for Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar [“chun-druh-SAY-kar”]. For 10 points, name these Earth-sized remnants of Sun-like stars.

tossups.p: Friedrich Bessel predicted in 1844 that a bright star had an unseen partner because of a wobble in its path, and Alvan Graham Clark spotted that partner in 1862 while testing a new telescope lens. That partner, nicknamed “the Pup,” is one of these objects.
tossups.r: It is Sirius B. For 10 points, name these dense, Earth-sized remnants of dead stars.

tossups.p: Willem Luyten coined the name of these objects in 1922. Astronomers give these objects spectral types beginning with the letter D, for “degenerate,” such as DA for the ones whose spectra show hydrogen.
tossups.r: Sirius B is one of these objects. For 10 points, name these hot but dim stellar remnants found at the lower left of the H–R diagram.

tossups.p: BPM 37093, one of these objects, was nicknamed “Lucy” after a Beatles song because its carbon core is thought to have crystallized into something like a giant diamond. Most of these objects are made mainly of carbon and oxygen, the ashes of helium fusion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these Earth-sized remnants, held up by electron degeneracy pressure, that the Sun will one day become.

tossups.p: Strangely, adding mass to one of these objects makes it shrink, because it must squeeze tighter before its electrons can push back hard enough against its stronger gravity. That push, called electron degeneracy pressure, comes from the Pauli exclusion principle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these dense remnants of Sun-like stars, which cannot weigh more than about 1.4 Suns.

tossups.p: When one of these objects pulls enough gas from a partner star to approach its mass limit, it can blow itself apart in a runaway burst of carbon fusion. Those Type Ia supernovae reach nearly the same peak brightness, so astronomers use them as standard candles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these Earth-sized stellar remnants, the leftover cores of stars like the Sun.

tossups.p: The recurrent nova RS Ophiuchi has flared up several times since 1898. In a nova, hydrogen that one of these objects has pulled from a partner star piles up on its surface until it ignites in a sudden burst of fusion, and this object survives to do it again.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hot, dim stellar remnants, such as Sirius B.

tossups.p: One of these objects sits at the center of the Ring Nebula in Lyra, lighting up the gas that its parent star blew off near the end of its life. Such glowing shells are called planetary nebulae, even though they have nothing to do with planets.
tossups.r: After its red giant stage, the Sun will become one of these objects. For 10 points, name these Earth-sized stellar remnants.

tossups.p: Because these objects no longer make energy by fusion, they slowly cool over billions of years, and in theory they will eventually fade into cold, dark “black dwarfs.” The universe is not yet old enough for any of these objects to have cooled that far.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hot but dim stellar remnants, found at the lower left of the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram.

tossups.p: By finding the faintest, coolest of these objects in a star cluster, astronomers can estimate the cluster’s age, since these objects cool at a predictable rate. More than 97 percent of the stars in the Milky Way, including the Sun, are expected to end up as these objects.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these dense stellar remnants, which are held up by electron pressure.

tossups.p: William Herschel first spotted 40 Eridani B in 1783, and in 1910, Williamina Fleming and her colleagues found that this dim star had the spectrum of a hot white star. Procyon B, the faint partner of the brightest star in Canis Minor, is another of these objects.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these tiny, hot stellar remnants, which include Sirius B.

tossups.p: In 1915, Walter Adams found that a faint partner of a bright star was hot and white, which meant that it had to be tiny and incredibly dense. A piece of one of these objects the size of a sugar cube would weigh about a ton.
tossups.r: That partner was Sirius B. For 10 points, name these Earth-sized remnants of Sun-like stars.

tossups.p: The strong gravity of these objects stretches the light leaving them to slightly longer wavelengths, an effect called gravitational redshift. Many of these objects are hotter than the Sun but give off far less light, because they are so small.
tossups.r: They sit at the lower left of the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram. For 10 points, name these stellar remnants about the size of Earth.

tossups.p: The atmospheres of many of these objects are “polluted” with metals such as iron and magnesium, which are thought to come from asteroids or planets torn apart by their strong gravity. Such heavy elements should sink out of sight fairly quickly, so the debris must have fallen in recently.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these Earth-sized remnants of Sun-like stars, held up by electron degeneracy pressure.

tossups.p: The heaviest of these objects may be made of oxygen, neon, and magnesium instead of carbon and oxygen. Stars with less than about eight times the Sun’s mass end their lives as these objects after puffing away their outer layers.
tossups.r: Sirius B is one. For 10 points, name these small, dense stellar remnants that the Sun will become.

trap.title: Which kind of dwarf?
trap.body: Astronomy is full of dwarfs. Red dwarfs are small, cool stars still fusing hydrogen; brown dwarfs are “failed stars” too small to fuse ordinary hydrogen; black dwarfs are what these objects would become after cooling for longer than the universe has existed; and the Sun itself is called a yellow dwarf. Neutron stars, the heavier leftovers of bigger stars, and novae and supernovae, which are explosions rather than objects, are the other common wrong buzzes.
trap.fix: Earth-sized, Sirius B, the Chandrasekhar limit, electron degeneracy pressure, or the star at the center of a planetary nebula means white dwarfs. City-sized and spinning, or pulsars, means neutron stars. Saying only “dwarf” earns a prompt, so always say “white.”
trap.line: Real answer line: white dwarfs (prompt on dwarfs; do not accept “red dwarfs,” “brown dwarfs,” or “black dwarfs”)

topics.name: Ceres
topics.kicker: Biggest body in the asteroid belt · Found in 1801, a dwarf planet since 2006
topics.dates: Discovered January 1, 1801; a dwarf planet since 2006
topics.briefing: On January 1, 1801, the first night of the 19th century, the Italian astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi, working in Palermo, Sicily, spotted a moving dot that turned out to be Ceres, the first object ever found in the asteroid belt. It was called a planet, then an asteroid, and since 2006 a dwarf planet. In 2015, NASA’s Dawn spacecraft arrived and found mysterious bright spots in a crater, made of salt left behind by salty water.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Cerealia Facula and Vinalia Faculae, the brightest spots on this world, are deposits of salt left behind by salty water that rose from below into the crater Occator. Those spots puzzled scientists when a spacecraft first approached this world in 2015.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this dwarf planet, the largest object in the asteroid belt.

tossups.p: While checking star positions for a catalog, a Theatine priest in Palermo spotted this object, which he cautiously reported as a possible comet. He named it for the patron goddess of Sicily.
tossups.r: That priest, Giuseppe Piazzi [“pee-AHT-see”], found it on January 1, 1801. For 10 points, name this first object discovered in the asteroid belt.

tossups.p: After this object disappeared into the Sun’s glare, a 24-year-old mathematician worked out its orbit so well that Franz Xaver von Zach and Heinrich Olbers found it again about a year after its discovery. That mathematician later explained his methods in an 1809 book on the motion of heavenly bodies.
tossups.r: He was Carl Friedrich Gauss. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet discovered in 1801.

tossups.p: In March 2015, a NASA spacecraft driven by xenon ion engines made this world the first dwarf planet ever orbited by a probe. That spacecraft had already spent more than a year orbiting Vesta.
tossups.r: That spacecraft was Dawn. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet, the largest object in the asteroid belt.

tossups.p: Ahuna Mons, a lone, steep-sided mountain on this world, is thought to be an ice volcano that pushed up icy, salty mud instead of molten rock. Ammonia-rich clays on this world’s surface hint that it may have formed farther from the Sun.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this dwarf planet in the asteroid belt, which NASA’s Dawn probe orbited.

tossups.p: In 2014, astronomers using the European Space Agency’s Herschel Space Observatory reported water vapor coming from this world. Scientists think a layer of salty water, or brine, may still lie deep beneath its crater Occator.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this dwarf planet, the only one in the inner solar system.

tossups.p: This object turned up close to where the Titius–Bode rule predicted a missing planet between Mars and Jupiter, just as a team nicknamed the “Celestial Police” was organizing a search for one. That team went on to find Pallas, Juno, and Vesta.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first asteroid to be discovered, found in 1801.

tossups.p: This object was listed as a planet for decades after its discovery, until so many similar bodies turned up that astronomers began calling them all asteroids instead. Unlike most of those bodies, it is massive enough to have pulled itself into a nearly round shape.
tossups.r: In 2006, the same vote that took away Pluto’s planet status made it a dwarf planet. For 10 points, name this largest object in the asteroid belt.

tossups.p: In 1803, the element cerium was named for this object, which had been discovered two years earlier. The word “cereal” comes from the same source as this object’s name.
tossups.r: This object is named for the Roman goddess of grain and farming. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet that Giuseppe Piazzi discovered in 1801.

tossups.p: Features on this world are named for farming gods and harvest festivals, and its famous crater Occator is named for a Roman god of harrowing, the breaking up of plowed soil. This world’s astronomical symbol is a sickle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this dwarf planet, named for the Roman goddess of agriculture.

tossups.p: About 940 kilometers across, this world is the smallest object officially recognized as a dwarf planet, yet it is massive enough that its own gravity has pulled it into a nearly round shape. Unlike Pluto, it orbits inside the orbit of Jupiter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this dwarf planet, the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

tossups.p: This object’s discoverer first wanted to add “Ferdinandea” to its name to honor King Ferdinand of Sicily, but only the first part stuck. That part honors the patron goddess of Sicily, where the discovery was made.
tossups.r: This object was found from Palermo in 1801. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet in the asteroid belt.

tossups.p: A NASA spacecraft ran out of fuel in 2018 while orbiting this world, after becoming the first spacecraft to orbit two different worlds beyond Earth. That probe was named for its goal of studying leftovers from the dawn of the solar system.
tossups.r: That probe, Dawn, had visited Vesta first. For 10 points, name this largest object in the asteroid belt.

tossups.p: This world takes about 4.6 years to orbit the Sun and spins once about every nine hours. It is far more massive than Vesta, the second-most massive object in its region, but Vesta usually looks brighter in our sky.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this dwarf planet in the asteroid belt, discovered by Giuseppe Piazzi.

tossups.p: William Herschel saw that this object and Pallas looked like mere points of light even in his best telescopes, so in 1802 he gave them a new group name from a Greek word meaning “star-like.”
tossups.r: That name is “asteroids.” For 10 points, name this object, the biggest asteroid, which is also a dwarf planet.

trap.title: Dwarf planet, asteroid, or goddess?
trap.body: Ceres is both the biggest asteroid and a dwarf planet, so its clues show up in tossups whose answer is “asteroids” in general, and real answer lines for that group do not accept Ceres. Vesta, the other world NASA’s Dawn probe orbited, and Pluto, which was reclassified by the same 2006 vote, are the other common wrong buzzes. In mythology questions, the Greek goddess of grain is Demeter, not Ceres.
trap.fix: “This object” or “this dwarf planet” plus Piazzi, Gauss, January 1, 1801, Occator’s bright spots, or Ahuna Mons means Ceres. “These objects” in the belt means asteroids. Vesta has a giant crater with a huge central mountain and is the brightest asteroid in our sky.

topics.name: The Sun
topics.kicker: The star at the center of our solar system · Powers nearly all life on Earth
topics.briefing: The Sun is a middle-aged yellow star that holds about 99.8 percent of all the mass in the solar system; about 109 Earths could line up across its face. In its core, at about 15 million degrees, it fuses hydrogen into helium and gives off about 3.8 × 10²⁶ watts. Its light takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth, so we always see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes earlier.
topics.answerHtml: the Sun (accept Sol; prompt on star or yellow dwarf; do not accept “sunspots” or “Helios”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The outer atmosphere of this star, its corona, is more than a million degrees, far hotter than its visible surface, a puzzle called the coronal heating problem. In 2021, a NASA probe named for Eugene Parker became the first spacecraft to fly through that corona.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this star that Earth orbits once a year.

tossups.p: Starting in the late 1960s, Raymond Davis caught neutrinos from this star with a huge tank of dry-cleaning fluid in the Homestake Mine in South Dakota, but he found only about a third of the number predicted. Neutrinos changing type on their way to Earth explained that shortfall.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this star, about 150 million kilometers from Earth.

tossups.p: In the 1800s, Lord Kelvin argued that this object could be only tens of millions of years old, because he assumed it shone by slowly shrinking under its own gravity. In 1920, Arthur Eddington suggested that it is powered instead by turning hydrogen into helium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this star, whose light takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.

tossups.p: In 1814, Joseph von Fraunhofer mapped hundreds of dark lines in this object’s spectrum. In 1868, astronomers studying its spectrum during an eclipse found a yellow line from an element not yet known on Earth, which was later named from this object’s Greek name.
tossups.r: That element is helium. For 10 points, name this star at the center of Earth’s planetary system.

tossups.p: About three-quarters of this object’s mass is hydrogen and about one-quarter is helium. Its visible surface, the photosphere, is about 5,500 degrees Celsius, while its core is thousands of times hotter.
tossups.r: It holds about 99.8 percent of the mass of its planetary system. For 10 points, name this yellow, G-type star that Earth orbits.

tossups.p: This object spins faster at its equator, about once every 25 days, than near its poles, where one turn takes about 35 days. The number of dark, cooler spots on its surface rises and falls over a cycle of about 11 years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this star, whose core is about 15 million kelvins.

tossups.p: This star lies about 26,000 light-years from the center of the Milky Way, in a minor spiral arm called the Orion Arm, and it takes about 230 million years to circle the galaxy once.
tossups.r: Earth orbits it once a year at a distance of one astronomical unit. For 10 points, name this star.

tossups.p: Energy made in this object’s core can take many thousands of years to work its way out through the radiative zone. It then rises through a convective zone, whose bubbling tops appear as granules on this object’s visible surface, the photosphere.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this star, which fuses hydrogen into helium in a core at about 15 million kelvins.

tossups.p: In 1958, Eugene Parker predicted that this object constantly blows a stream of charged particles into space, and in 2012, Voyager 1 left the giant bubble carved out by that stream. Those particles help light up auroras when they reach Earth.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this star whose wind streams past all of its planets.

tossups.p: In 1859, Richard Carrington saw a brilliant white-light flare on this object, and within a day a huge storm of charged particles made telegraph wires spark and auroras glow near the tropics. Giant eruptions of gas from this object are called coronal mass ejections.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this star, whose outbursts cause space weather around Earth.

tossups.p: Aristarchus of Samos proposed in the third century BCE that Earth circles this object, an idea that Nicolaus Copernicus revived in his 1543 book _On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this star at the center of the model that replaced Ptolemy’s Earth-centered system.

tossups.p: Hans Bethe won a Nobel Prize for working out the nuclear reactions that power this object and other stars. This object turns about four million tons of its mass into energy every second, for a total power output of about 3.8 times 10 to the 26th watts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this star, whose light reaches Earth in about eight minutes.

tossups.p: During a 1919 eclipse, Arthur Eddington’s expedition measured starlight bending around this object, supporting Albert Einstein’s general relativity. Its pearly corona can be seen with the naked eye only during a total eclipse, such as the one that crossed North America on April 8, 2024.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this star, which the Moon blocks during a total eclipse.

tossups.p: Early in its life, this star gave off only about 70 percent as much energy as it does in modern times, yet young Earth still had liquid water. In about five billion years, it will swell into a red giant, and it will end its life as a white dwarf.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this G2 V star, which is about 4.6 billion years old.

tossups.p: This object’s astronomical symbol is a circle with a dot at its center. Greek myths pictured its god Helios driving a fiery chariot across the sky each day, and the ancient Egyptians worshipped it as Ra.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this star, the source of daylight on Earth.

clues.t: The star at the center of our planetary system, which Earth orbits once a year
About 150 million km (93 million miles) away, so its light takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth
Fuses hydrogen into helium in its core, at about 15 million kelvins
A G-type main-sequence star, or yellow dwarf; its full label is G2 V
Holds about 99.8 percent of the mass in its planetary system; about 109 Earths could line up across its face
About 4.6 billion years old; in about five billion years it will swell into a red giant, then end as a white dwarf
Layers from the inside out: core, radiative zone, convective zone, photosphere (the visible surface), chromosphere, and corona
Its outer atmosphere, the corona, is more than a million degrees, far hotter than its surface (about 5,500 °C)
Blows a constant stream of charged particles, called its wind, which helps light up auroras on Earth
Gives off about 3.8 × 10²⁶ watts; about 1,361 watts per square meter reach the top of Earth’s atmosphere
Dark, cooler magnetic spots on its surface rise and fall in number over a cycle of about 11 years
Nicolaus Copernicus put it at the center of his model in 1543; Aristarchus of Samos had proposed the idea in the third century BCE
Helium was found in its spectrum during an 1868 eclipse, before it was found on Earth, and was named from its Greek name
Its corona can be seen with the naked eye only during a total eclipse, like the one across North America on April 8, 2024
Why the corona is so much hotter than the surface is the coronal heating problem; in 2021, a NASA probe named for Eugene Parker first flew through the corona
Eugene Parker predicted its wind in 1958; Voyager 1 left the giant bubble carved out by that wind in 2012
Raymond Davis’s tank of dry-cleaning fluid in South Dakota’s Homestake Mine caught only about a third of its predicted neutrinos; neutrinos changing type explained why
Lord Kelvin thought it could be only tens of millions of years old, assuming it shone by slowly shrinking under gravity
Arthur Eddington proposed in 1920 that it runs on hydrogen turning into helium; Hans Bethe later won a Nobel Prize for working out the reactions
Joseph von Fraunhofer mapped hundreds of dark lines in its spectrum in 1814
Spins about once every 25 days at its equator but only about once every 35 days near its poles
About 26,000 light-years from the Milky Way’s center, in the Orion Arm; one trip around the galaxy takes about 230 million years
Richard Carrington saw a white-light flare on it in 1859; within a day, a huge storm made telegraph wires spark
Energy from its core can take many thousands of years to cross the radiative zone; convection makes granules on its surface
Turns about four million tons of its mass into energy every second
Early in its life it gave off only about 70 percent of its modern energy, yet young Earth had liquid water
Its symbol is a circle with a dot in the center; the Greek god Helios drove its chariot, and Egyptians worshipped it as Ra
Arthur Eddington’s 1919 eclipse expedition measured starlight bending around it, supporting Einstein’s general relativity

trap.title: Star, spots, or god?
trap.body: Sunspots have their own answer line, and their clues (dark, cooler patches, the 11-year cycle, the Maunder Minimum) also turn up in tossups about the whole star, so players blurt out “sunspots.” Others hear “nearest star” and say Proxima Centauri, which is only the nearest star beyond this one. In mythology, Helios and Ra are gods of this star, a different answer line.
trap.fix: “This star” or “this object” plus Earth’s orbit, eight-minute light travel, the corona, Eugene Parker, Raymond Davis’s neutrinos, or Fraunhofer lines means the Sun. “These dark regions” means sunspots. You can also answer “Sol,” its Latin name.
trap.line: Real answer line: the Sun (accept Sol; prompt on star)

topics.name: Big Bang
topics.kicker: How the universe began, hot and dense · Expanding for about 13.8 billion years
topics.dates: About 13.8 billion years ago; named in 1949
topics.briefing: The Big Bang theory says that about 13.8 billion years ago, the whole universe was in an incredibly hot, dense state, and it has been expanding and cooling ever since. It was not an explosion at one spot in space but a stretching of space itself, everywhere at once. The astronomer Fred Hoyle, who preferred a rival theory, gave it its catchy name on BBC radio in 1949.
topics.answerHtml: Big Bang theory (accept Big Bang model or cosmology; prompt on primeval atom or expanding universe; do not accept “cosmic microwave background,” “inflation,” or “Steady State theory”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: When a Belgian priest showed him math suggesting that the universe might be expanding, Albert Einstein reportedly said the math was correct but the physics was “abominable.” That priest, Georges Lemaître [“luh-MET-ruh”], later said the universe began as a single “primeval atom.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in a hot, dense state.

tossups.p: Hermann Bondi, Thomas Gold, and Fred Hoyle championed a rival to this theory, in which new matter is constantly created as the universe expands, so that the universe always looks the same. That rival model was called the Steady State theory.
tossups.r: Hoyle himself coined this theory’s name on BBC radio in 1949. For 10 points, name this theory that the universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense beginning.

tossups.p: As a pun on the first three letters of the Greek alphabet, George Gamow [“GAM-off”] added Hans Bethe’s name to a 1948 paper with Ralph Alpher about how the chemical elements formed. Alpher and Robert Herman also predicted that leftover radiation from this event should still fill space.
tossups.r: That radiation is the cosmic microwave background. For 10 points, name this event that began the universe about 13.8 billion years ago.

tossups.p: In the first few minutes after this event, protons and neutrons fused to make most of the universe’s helium, which makes up about a quarter of all ordinary matter by mass, along with a tiny bit of lithium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event that started the expansion of the universe about 13.8 billion years ago.

tossups.p: To explain why the universe looks so smooth in every direction and why space is so nearly flat, physicists propose that a split second after this event, the universe swelled enormously in a burst called inflation. Alan Guth proposed that idea around 1980.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event, the hot, dense beginning of the universe about 13.8 billion years ago.

tossups.p: In 1922, Alexander Friedmann found solutions to Albert Einstein’s equations that describe an expanding universe, ideas that later fed into this theory. Einstein himself had at first preferred a universe that stays the same size.
tossups.r: Edwin Hubble’s 1929 discovery that distant galaxies are rushing away from us became key evidence for it. For 10 points, name this theory of the universe’s origin.

tossups.p: Olbers’ paradox asks why the night sky is dark if the universe is endless and filled with stars, and part of the answer comes from this theory: the universe has a limited age, so light from the most distant stars has not had time to reach us.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago.

tossups.p: Robert Dicke’s team at Princeton was building an instrument to search for radiation left over from this event when they learned that two Bell Labs scientists had already found it by accident. That faint glow was released about 380,000 years after this event.
tossups.r: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered it in 1964. For 10 points, name this event that began the universe, named by Fred Hoyle.

tossups.p: Physicists call the first tiny sliver of time after this event, up to about 10 to the minus 43rd seconds, the Planck epoch. For the first several microseconds after this event, the universe was filled with a hot soup of quarks and gluons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event, the hot, dense beginning of the universe.

tossups.p: Stephen Hawking and Roger Penrose argued that, if general relativity holds, this event must have started from a singularity, a point of infinite density. Hawking’s 1966 Cambridge thesis made an early version of that argument.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event that began the expansion of the universe about 13.8 billion years ago.

tossups.p: For about 380,000 years after this event, the universe was a glowing fog of plasma that light could not pass through, until it cooled enough for electrons and nuclei to join into neutral atoms. Most of those first atoms were hydrogen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event, the beginning of the universe in a hot, dense state.

tossups.p: Cosmologists contrast this event with possible endings for the universe nicknamed the Big Freeze, the Big Rip, and the Big Crunch, which would be like this event run in reverse. In 1998, astronomers found that the expansion that began with this event is speeding up.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event that began the universe about 13.8 billion years ago.

tossups.p: Quasars, which are common far away but rare nearby, supported this theory because they show that the universe has changed over time. The discovery of those faraway objects in the 1960s was a blow to the rival Steady State theory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory, which says the universe expanded from a hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago.

tossups.p: In 1927, two years before Edwin Hubble’s famous paper, Georges Lemaître published his own estimate of how fast the universe is expanding, a key step toward this theory. In 2018, the International Astronomical Union voted to recommend renaming the law describing that expansion to honor both men.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory of the universe’s origin, named by Fred Hoyle.

tossups.p: Unlike an ordinary explosion, this event did not happen at one spot in space; instead, space itself began stretching everywhere at once, so it has no center. A CBS sitcom about scientists at Caltech, which ran from 2007 to 2019, was named for this theory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event, the beginning of the universe about 13.8 billion years ago.

clues.t: Theory that the universe began in an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since
Happened about 13.8 billion years ago
Named by Fred Hoyle in a 1949 BBC radio broadcast, even though he favored a rival theory
Its leftover glow is the cosmic microwave background, found by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson in 1964
Edwin Hubble’s 1929 discovery that distant galaxies are rushing away from us is key evidence for it
First proposed by the Belgian priest Georges Lemaître, who said the universe began as a “primeval atom”
Its old rival, the Steady State theory of Hoyle, Hermann Bondi, and Thomas Gold, said new matter is constantly created
In its first few minutes, most of the universe’s helium formed (about a quarter of ordinary matter by mass), plus a little lithium
For about 380,000 years the universe was a fog of plasma; then neutral atoms, mostly hydrogen, formed and set free the light we see as the CMB
Around 1980, Alan Guth proposed that the universe swelled enormously in a split second just after it, an idea called inflation
Not an explosion at one spot in space: space itself began stretching everywhere at once, so there is no center
George Gamow added Hans Bethe’s name to his 1948 paper with Ralph Alpher on how the elements formed, as a pun on alpha, beta, gamma
Quasars, common far away but rare nearby, show that the universe has changed over time, evidence against the Steady State theory
A CBS sitcom about scientists at Caltech, which ran from 2007 to 2019, is named for it
Albert Einstein reportedly told Lemaître that his math was correct but his physics was “abominable”
Alexander Friedmann found expanding-universe solutions to Einstein’s equations in 1922; Einstein had at first preferred an unchanging universe
Robert Dicke’s Princeton team was about to search for its leftover radiation when two Bell Labs scientists found it by accident
Lemaître estimated the expansion rate in 1927, two years before Hubble; in 2018, astronomers voted to recommend renaming the expansion law for both men
Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman predicted in 1948 that its leftover radiation should still fill space, at about 5 kelvins
It helps answer Olbers’ paradox (why is the night sky dark?): the universe has a limited age
The first sliver of time after it, up to about 10⁻⁴³ seconds, is called the Planck epoch
For its first several microseconds, the universe was filled with a hot soup of quarks and gluons
Stephen Hawking and Roger Penrose argued it began with a singularity; Hawking’s 1966 Cambridge thesis made an early version of the case
Possible endings of the universe contrasted with it: the Big Freeze, the Big Rip, and the Big Crunch (like it run in reverse)
In 1998, astronomers found that the expansion it began is speeding up, which is blamed on dark energy
Inflation helps explain why the universe looks so smooth in every direction and why space is so nearly flat

trap.title: Theory, glow, or inflation?
trap.body: Tossups on the cosmic microwave background usually end by calling it the afterglow of this event, and tossups on this event mention that glow, so players mix up the two answer lines. Inflation, Alan Guth’s idea of a split-second growth spurt just after the beginning, is a separate answer line too, and so is Hubble’s law. The Steady State theory of Fred Hoyle, Hermann Bondi, and Thomas Gold was the rival idea.
trap.fix: “This theory” or “this event” plus Lemaître’s primeval atom, Hoyle’s 1949 nickname, 13.8 billion years, or the first few minutes of element-making means the Big Bang. “This radiation” or “this glow” found by Penzias and Wilson means the cosmic microwave background. A brief period of extremely rapid expansion means inflation.
trap.line: Real answer line: Big Bang theory (prompt on primeval atom; do not accept “cosmic microwave background” or “Steady State theory”)

topics.name: Triton
topics.kicker: Neptune’s largest moon · Orbits backward and sprays nitrogen geysers
topics.briefing: Triton, Neptune’s largest moon, does something no other big moon does: it orbits backward, opposite to the way its planet spins. That strange orbit suggests that Neptune captured it from the Kuiper belt long ago. When Voyager 2 flew past in 1989, it found one of the coldest surfaces in the solar system, a pinkish landscape where geysers shoot nitrogen gas several kilometers high.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The discoverer of this moon later found two moons of Uranus, Ariel and Umbriel. That discoverer, William Lassell, an English brewer who built his own telescopes, found this moon just 17 days after its planet was found in 1846.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this largest moon of Neptune, which orbits backward.

tossups.p: A large region of this moon is covered in dimpled, wrinkled ground nicknamed “cantaloupe terrain” because it looks like the skin of a melon. This moon has very few craters, which shows that its surface is geologically young.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this largest moon of Neptune, which Voyager 2 photographed in 1989.

tossups.p: In 1989, Voyager 2 spotted dark plumes rising up to about 8 kilometers above this moon’s icy surface, where geysers shoot out nitrogen gas carrying dark dust. Winds in this moon’s thin atmosphere smear that dust into long streaks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this moon of Neptune, which orbits in the opposite direction from its planet’s spin.

tossups.p: Tides from its planet are slowly shrinking this moon’s orbit, so billions of years in the future it may be torn apart into a ring or crash into its planet. That fate comes from the unusual direction of this moon’s orbit.
tossups.r: It orbits opposite to its planet’s spin. For 10 points, name this backward-orbiting largest moon of Neptune.

tossups.p: One idea says this moon was once half of a pair of icy bodies that broke up when it swung close to its planet, which then captured it. That capture may have disturbed the planet’s other moons, flinging Nereid into a stretched-out orbit.
tossups.r: It probably came from the Kuiper belt. For 10 points, name this largest moon of Neptune, which orbits backward.

tossups.p: Voyager 2 measured this moon’s surface at about minus 235 degrees Celsius, one of the coldest temperatures ever measured in the solar system. Its surface is mostly frozen nitrogen, with water ice and frozen carbon dioxide.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this largest moon of Neptune, discovered by William Lassell.

tossups.p: This moon is somewhat larger than Pluto, and the two worlds have similar densities and nitrogen-rich icy surfaces, which suggests that they formed in the same region of space. It is the seventh-largest moon in the solar system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this moon of Neptune, which may be a captured Kuiper belt object.

tossups.p: Camille Flammarion suggested this moon’s name in 1880, borrowing it from a sea god who blew a conch shell to calm or stir up the waves.
tossups.r: In Greek myth, that merman was a son of Poseidon. For 10 points, name this largest moon of Neptune.

tossups.p: This world’s large southern polar cap of nitrogen ice looks pinkish and is streaked with dark material blown out by geysers. Beneath its icy crust, this world is thought to have a large rocky core.
tossups.r: Voyager 2 photographed it in August 1989, near the end of its grand tour. For 10 points, name this largest moon of Neptune.

tossups.p: Some scientists think an ocean of liquid water may lie hidden beneath this moon’s icy crust, which would make it a target in the search for life. This moon also has a very thin atmosphere of nitrogen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this largest moon of Neptune, which orbits in a retrograde direction.

tossups.p: This moon holds more than 99 percent of the mass of everything orbiting its planet, and it is the only one of that planet’s moons big enough to have pulled itself into a round shape.
tossups.r: Voyager 2 photographed it in 1989. For 10 points, name this largest moon of Neptune.

tossups.p: This moon always keeps the same face toward its planet and takes about six days to complete each orbit, which is tilted compared with its planet’s equator.
tossups.r: Its orbit runs backward. For 10 points, name this moon of Neptune, found by William Lassell in 1846.

tossups.p: The amateur astronomer who discovered this moon had made his fortune brewing beer in Liverpool, and he later moved a large telescope to the island of Malta to escape cloudy English skies.
tossups.r: That astronomer, William Lassell, found it in 1846. For 10 points, name this largest moon of Neptune.

tossups.p: Along with Saturn’s moon Enceladus, this moon is one of the few icy worlds where spacecraft have seen active eruptions, a kind of activity called cryovolcanism. Its geysers may be powered by weak sunlight warming nitrogen ice from below, like a greenhouse.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this moon of Neptune where Voyager 2 spotted nitrogen geysers.

tossups.p: For about a century after its discovery, this moon was usually just called “the satellite of Neptune,” because it was that planet’s only known moon until Gerard Kuiper found Nereid in 1949.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this largest moon of Neptune, which has a retrograde orbit.

Orbits backward (retrograde), opposite to its planet’s spin: the only large moon in the solar system that does
Voyager 2 photographed it in August 1989, just after passing Neptune

Voyager 2 saw geysers shooting nitrogen gas; winds in its thin atmosphere smear their dust into dark streaks
Probably a captured Kuiper belt object, which explains its backward orbit
Discovered by William Lassell in 1846, just 17 days after Neptune itself was found
One of the coldest surfaces ever measured in the solar system, about −235 °C
Its surface is mostly frozen nitrogen, with water ice and frozen carbon dioxide, over a large rocky core; its south polar cap looks pinkish
Somewhat larger than Pluto, with a similar density and icy surface; the seventh-largest moon in the solar system
Has very few craters, so its surface is geologically young
A large region is covered in dimpled, wrinkled “cantaloupe terrain,” like the skin of a melon
Its discoverer, Lassell, was a Liverpool brewer who built his own telescopes and later moved a large one to Malta
Lassell also discovered Uranus’s moons Ariel and Umbriel (1851)
Tides are slowly shrinking its orbit; billions of years in the future it may be torn into a ring or crash into Neptune
May once have been one member of a pair of Kuiper belt objects; its capture may have flung Nereid into a stretched-out orbit
Camille Flammarion suggested its name in 1880; the merman it is named for blew a conch shell to calm or stir up the waves
For about a century it was usually just called “the satellite of Neptune,” until Gerard Kuiper found Nereid in 1949
Its dark plumes rise up to about 8 km above the surface
Some scientists think an ocean of liquid water may lie beneath its icy crust
Holds more than 99 percent of the mass of everything orbiting Neptune, and it is Neptune’s only moon big enough to be round
Always keeps the same face toward Neptune and takes about six days per orbit, which is tilted compared with Neptune’s equator
With Saturn’s Enceladus, one of the few icy worlds where spacecraft have seen active eruptions (cryovolcanism)
Its geysers may be powered by weak sunlight warming nitrogen ice from below, like a greenhouse

trap.title: Triton, Titan, or Neptune?
trap.body: Triton sounds a lot like Titan, Saturn’s largest moon, and Titania, Uranus’s largest moon, and players under pressure mix them up. Neptune tossups are also full of Triton clues, so it is easy to name the moon when the question wants the planet, or the planet when it wants the moon. In mythology, Triton is Poseidon’s son, a separate answer from Poseidon himself.
trap.fix: A backward orbit, nitrogen geysers, cantaloupe terrain, William Lassell in 1846, or a captured Kuiper belt object means Triton. A thick orange haze, methane lakes, or the Huygens probe means Titan. Listen for the noun: “this moon” means Triton, while “this planet” means Neptune.
trap.line: Real answer line: Triton (do not accept “Titan” or “Neptune”)

topics.name: Cepheid variables
topics.kicker: Pulsing stars that reveal their true brightness · Yardsticks for the universe
topics.briefing: Cepheid variables are giant stars that swell and shrink like a beating heart, brightening and dimming on a regular schedule of days or weeks. In 1912, Henrietta Swan Leavitt discovered that the slower a Cepheid pulses, the more light it truly gives off, so astronomers can work out how far away it is. Edwin Hubble used that rule to show that the Andromeda “nebula” is a separate galaxy.
topics.answerHtml: Cepheid variables (accept Cepheids or Delta Cephei variables; prompt on variable stars, pulsating stars, or standard candles; do not accept “Cepheus,” “RR Lyrae,” or “Polaris”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Edward Pigott found one of these stars, Eta Aquilae, in 1784, the same year that his deaf young friend John Goodricke noticed that a star in the constellation of a mythical king brightened and dimmed every five days or so.
tossups.r: Goodricke’s star, Delta Cephei, names this class. For 10 points, name these pulsating stars used as standard candles.

tossups.p: While studying photographic plates of the Small Magellanic Cloud, a Harvard “computer” realized that she could compare these stars fairly, because all of them lie at about the same distance from Earth. She hinted at her famous pattern in 1908 and confirmed it in 1912.
tossups.r: That astronomer, Henrietta Swan Leavitt [“LEV-it”], found that the longer these stars take to pulse, the brighter they are. For 10 points, name these pulsating stars.

tossups.p: After photographing the Andromeda “nebula” in October 1923, Edwin Hubble crossed out the letter “N” on the plate and wrote “VAR!” when he realized that a star he had marked as a nova was really one of these stars.
tossups.r: That star proved that Andromeda is a separate galaxy. For 10 points, name these pulsating stars that serve as standard candles.

tossups.p: Walter Baade [“BAH-duh”] showed in 1952 that these stars come in two types that differ in brightness, which meant that distances to other galaxies were roughly twice what Edwin Hubble had measured.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these pulsating stars that follow Henrietta Leavitt’s period–luminosity law.

tossups.p: These stars pulse because of the kappa mechanism, in which a layer of partly ionized helium soaks up heat when it is squeezed and lets it out when it expands, working like a valve that Arthur Eddington first imagined.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these yellow giant stars that brighten and dim in regular cycles, named for Delta Cephei.

tossups.p: Polaris, the North Star, is the closest of these stars to Earth, though its brightness changes only slightly over a cycle of about four days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these pulsating stars whose periods reveal their true brightness, named for Delta Cephei.

tossups.p: In 1914, Harlow Shapley argued that these stars change brightness because they pulse in and out, not because they are pairs of stars eclipsing each other. Shapley later used variable stars in globular clusters to show that the Sun lies far from the center of the Milky Way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these pulsating stars, used as standard candles.

tossups.p: On the H–R diagram, these stars lie in a narrow region called the instability strip, which also holds RR Lyrae [“LY-ree”] stars. Classical examples of these stars are yellow supergiants, far more luminous than the Sun.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these pulsating stars whose periods reveal their luminosity.

tossups.p: In 1925, the Swedish mathematician Gösta Mittag-Leffler wrote to the astronomer who discovered a key rule about these stars, hoping to nominate her for a Nobel Prize, without knowing that she had died years earlier.
tossups.r: That astronomer was Henrietta Swan Leavitt. For 10 points, name these pulsating stars used to measure distances to galaxies.

tossups.p: Expansion rates for the universe measured with these stars and supernovae disagree with values worked out from the cosmic microwave background, a puzzle called the Hubble tension. The Hubble Space Telescope’s Key Project studied these stars in galaxies millions of light-years away.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these pulsating stars, which work as standard candles.

tossups.p: As these stars pulse, Doppler shifts in their spectra show their surfaces moving toward and away from us, and their surface temperatures change over each cycle, too. Their cycles range from about a day to a few months.
tossups.r: Longer-period ones are more luminous. For 10 points, name these pulsating stars named for Delta Cephei.

tossups.p: In 1913, Ejnar Hertzsprung worked out distances to a few nearby examples of these stars, which turned Henrietta Leavitt’s rule into a tool for measuring distances across space.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these pulsating stars whose periods reveal how bright they truly are.

tossups.p: One astronomer who studied these stars lost much of her hearing and discovered more than 2,000 variable stars, but the 1912 report announcing her famous rule about these stars was signed by her boss at Harvard, Edward Pickering.
tossups.r: She was Henrietta Swan Leavitt. For 10 points, name these stars, whose periods reveal how bright they truly are.

tossups.p: On the cosmic distance ladder, these stars form the rung just above parallax, and astronomers use them to check the true brightness of Type Ia supernovae in nearby galaxies.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these stars that brighten and dim in a regular cycle whose period reveals their luminosity.

tossups.p: The same deaf astronomer who discovered that the namesake of these stars changes in brightness had earlier suggested that the star Algol dims because a darker companion passes in front of it.
tossups.r: That astronomer, John Goodricke, noticed Delta Cephei’s changes in 1784. For 10 points, name these pulsating stars used as standard candles.

trap.title: Which variable star?
trap.body: Several kinds of variable stars show up in astronomy tossups. RR Lyrae stars also pulse and also work as standard candles, but their cycles last less than a day. Mira variables are cool red giants with cycles of many months, and eclipsing binaries such as Algol dim only because one star passes in front of the other. Players also blurt out “Henrietta Leavitt” or “Polaris,” a person and a single example, when the question wants the whole class of stars.
trap.fix: Leavitt’s period–luminosity law, Delta Cephei, John Goodricke, Hubble’s “VAR!” star in Andromeda, or Walter Baade’s two types means Cepheid variables. Cycles shorter than a day in old globular clusters point to RR Lyrae stars. Saying only “variable stars” earns a prompt, so add “Cepheid.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Cepheid variables (accept Cepheids; prompt on variable stars; do not accept “RR Lyrae”)

topics.name: Kuiper Belt
topics.kicker: Icy ring of worlds beyond Neptune · Home of Pluto and snowman-shaped Arrokoth
topics.dates: Predicted 1940s–1951; first object beyond Pluto and Charon found 1992
topics.briefing: Far beyond Neptune, a wide, doughnut-shaped ring of icy leftovers from the birth of the solar system circles the Sun: the Kuiper belt. Pluto was its first member found, in 1930, but apart from Pluto’s moon Charon, nobody spotted another one until 1992. Since then, astronomers have found thousands, and on New Year’s Day 2019, NASA’s New Horizons probe flew past one called Arrokoth, which is shaped like a snowman.
topics.answerHtml: Kuiper belt (accept Edgeworth–Kuiper belt; prompt on Kuiper alone or trans-Neptunian objects; do not accept “Oort cloud,” “asteroid belt,” or “scattered disk”)

tossups.p: Objects with nearly circular orbits in this region are nicknamed “cubewanos,” a name taken from the label of the first object found here after Pluto and Charon, 1992 QB1. That object was later named Albion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belt of icy bodies beyond Neptune, home to Pluto.

tossups.p: In 2012, David Jewitt and Jane Luu shared the Kavli Prize with Mike Brown. After searching for about five years, Jewitt and Luu had used a telescope on Mauna Kea in Hawaii to find the first known object in this region besides Pluto and Charon, in 1992.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this region of icy bodies beyond Neptune, named for a Dutch-American astronomer.

tossups.p: In 1951, a Dutch-American astronomer wrote about a disk of icy bodies beyond the planets, though he thought it might have been cleared out long ago. A few years earlier, the Irish astronomer Kenneth Edgeworth had suggested that such a reservoir existed.
tossups.r: That astronomer was Gerard Kuiper [“KY-per”]. For 10 points, name this region beyond Neptune that contains Pluto.

tossups.p: Arrokoth, whose name means “sky” in the Powhatan language, is an object in this region that looks like a flattened snowman, made of two lobes that gently stuck together. Once nicknamed “Ultima Thule,” it was visited by a NASA probe on January 1, 2019.
tossups.r: That probe was New Horizons. For 10 points, name this belt of icy bodies beyond Neptune.

tossups.p: Objects in this region that orbit the Sun twice for every three orbits of Neptune are called plutinos, after their most famous member. Neptune’s gravity also herds other objects here into similar resonances.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this region of icy bodies beyond Neptune, which includes Pluto.

tossups.p: The number of objects in this region drops sharply at about 50 times Earth’s distance from the Sun, an edge nicknamed a “cliff.” Most of this region lies between about 30 and 50 astronomical units from the Sun.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disk of icy bodies just beyond Neptune’s orbit.

tossups.p: Many short-period comets, such as the Jupiter-family comets, are thought to begin as icy bodies in this region or in the scattered disk just beyond it. Long-period comets come from the much more distant Oort cloud instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this region of icy bodies beyond Neptune, named partly for Gerard Kuiper.

tossups.p: This region holds the dwarf planet Haumea, which is stretched into an egg shape by its fast spin of about four hours, and Makemake, which was discovered just after Easter in 2005 and named for a god of Easter Island’s Rapa Nui people.
tossups.r: Pluto also lies in it. For 10 points, name this belt of icy bodies beyond Neptune.

tossups.p: Mike Brown wrote _How I Killed Pluto and Why It Had It Coming_ about finding Eris, a dwarf planet that orbits mostly in the scattered disk just beyond this region. The discovery of Eris in 2005 helped get Pluto reclassified.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this region beyond Neptune, home to Pluto, Haumea, and Makemake.

tossups.p: Neptune’s large moon Triton, which orbits backward, is probably an object captured from this region. Like Pluto, the objects here are mostly mixtures of rock and frozen water, methane, and ammonia, leftovers from the formation of the solar system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belt of icy bodies beyond Neptune.

tossups.p: This region is about 20 times as wide as the asteroid belt and much more massive, yet all of its objects together likely add up to only a small fraction of Earth’s mass.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this doughnut-shaped region of icy bodies beyond Neptune, home to Pluto.

tossups.p: In the Nice [“NEESS”] model, named for a city in France, the giant planets moved after they formed, and Neptune’s outward drift scattered and sculpted the objects of this region. Neptune’s gravity still shapes the orbits of many objects here.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this region of icy bodies just beyond Neptune, which contains Pluto.

tossups.p: Quaoar [“KWAH-wahr”], an object in this region, was found in 2023 to have a ring far outside the distance where rings were expected to survive. Another object here, Orcus, is nicknamed the “anti-Pluto” because it moves in a similar orbit but on the opposite side of the Sun.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belt of icy bodies beyond Neptune.

tossups.p: NASA’s New Horizons, launched in January 2006, was the first spacecraft sent to explore this region, and its team used the Hubble Space Telescope in 2014 to find a second target here, Arrokoth.
tossups.r: New Horizons flew past this region’s best-known member, Pluto, in 2015. For 10 points, name this belt of icy worlds beyond Neptune.

tossups.p: The “cold classical” objects of this region have nearly circular, barely tilted orbits and probably formed in place, and many of them come in pairs. Arrokoth is one of those cold classical objects.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belt of icy bodies beyond Neptune, named for Gerard Kuiper and Kenneth Edgeworth.

trap.title: Kuiper belt or Oort cloud?
trap.body: The solar system has two icy reservoirs. The Kuiper belt is a doughnut-shaped ring just beyond Neptune, about 30 to 50 AU from the Sun, while the Oort cloud is a far more distant, roughly round shell that sends in long-period comets and has never been seen directly. Players also blurt out “asteroid belt,” the rocky ring between Mars and Jupiter, or “scattered disk,” the region of stretched-out orbits where Eris spends most of its time.
trap.fix: Pluto, plutinos, Arrokoth, New Horizons, 1992 QB1, Jewitt and Luu, or short-period comets mean the Kuiper belt. Ernst Öpik, Jan Oort, a round shell, or long-period comets mean the Oort cloud. Ceres, Vesta, and Kirkwood gaps mean the asteroid belt. Saying only “Kuiper” earns a prompt, so add “belt.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Kuiper belt (accept Edgeworth–Kuiper belt; do not accept “Oort cloud” or “asteroid belt”)
